intro: The reverse of Isabelle Nef’s Oiseau-Lyre disc has a gigue by Élisabeth Jacquet de La Guerre. The first strain is played twice, and the second strain, played once, is longer than either playing of the first.

sections.label: A · First strain, repeated
sections.mNote: The first strain, played a second time.

cues.title: Gigue, first strain
cues.text: The gigue is a quick dance in compound time, written in two strains. The harpsichord plays the first strain.
cues.evidence: The gigues of Jacquet de La Guerre’s 1687 book are each in two strains (Steve Wiberg’s edition, Due West Editions, 2007, from a facsimile of the first printing, IMSLP 18522, printed pages 7, 19, 20, 28 and 40): http://conquest.imslp.info/files/imglnks/usimg/3/31/IMSLP18522-LaGuerre_PiecesDeClavecin_Complete.pdf . The printed source of this gigue is not identified.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: First strain repeated
cues.text: The first strain is played again from its beginning before the second strain starts.
cues.evidence: The recording plays the first strain twice, with a dip in level before the repeat.

cues.title: Second strain
cues.text: The second strain begins with a new attack after a dip in level. It takes up the rest of the performance and is longer than either pass of the first strain.
cues.evidence: The recording dips in level and restarts at this point, and the second strain is not repeated.

cues.title: Closing attack
cues.text: The last bars are quieter, and the dance closes on a final louder attack.
cues.evidence: The recording’s level falls through the last bars and then rises sharply at the final attack, which ends the performance.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Bibliothèque nationale de France record reads “Isabelle Nef, clav.” and gives her dates as 1898–1976. The make of the instrument is not established.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: A gigue by Jacquet de La Guerre for harpsichord; the printed source (book and suite) is not identified
fields.note: The labels and the Internet Archive record name only an Allemande and a Gigue by Elizabeth Jacquet de la Guerre. An earlier comparison of pitch content with the printed gigues of the 1687 book proposed the F major gigue (EJG.04) and could not be reproduced. Re-measured for this review with the mains hum removed, the pitch content is centred on A minor (G♯ present, B♭ rare) and the first strain ends on an E harmony with G♯, which does not fit an F major piece. The gigue of the A minor suite (EJG.03, printed page 28) is a candidate that was matched only on key and first-strain cadence. The Allemande on the reverse sounds in G major, so the two sides may come from different suites. The 1707 book (EJG.05–06) was not compared, because its scan could not be downloaded.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The recording date is not stated in the sources consulted. The BnF record dates the disc 1942; an Oiseau-Lyre discography after Jim Davidson’s Lyrebird Rising (1994) gives its release as 1938 or 1939, recording site and date unknown (https://medieval.org/emfaq/cds/lol75.htm). The Internet Archive upload date of 25 October 2018 is not a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No recording venue is established by the sources.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Named as publisher in the Internet Archive item. The label issued its first 78 rpm discs in December 1937.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Internet Archive description gives “Catalog number: O. L. 75”, and the label scan reads “O. L. 75” on both sides.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: PART 1296 (Gigue); the reverse side, the Allemande, is PART 1295
fields.note: Matrix numbers are taken from the item’s external identifiers. No take is supplied.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: George Blood, L.P., for the Internet Archive’s 78 rpm project (Boston Public Library collection)
fields.note: The item’s description names an audio engineer at George Blood, L.P., and lists the item in the Boston Public Library and George Blood collections.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The upload date of 25 October 2018 is not treated as a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Digitised at 78 rpm with four stylus sizes, flat and equalised; the engineer’s preferred version is the one offered, as a variable-bitrate MP3 derived from a 24-bit FLAC.
fields.note: The pitch of the file, re-measured for this review, is about 25 cents above A = 440, as on the other side of the disc. The written key of the piece is not established, so the transfer speed cannot be checked against a score; no speed correction was applied here.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Jacquet de La Guerre died in 1729. This is a term calculation, not clearance of every edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis for a disc dated 1942 by the Bibliothèque nationale de France (release in 1938 or 1939 according to an Oiseau-Lyre discography), under the programme’s pre-1963 recording rule.
fields.note: The BnF date is a catalogue date for the disc, not an independently verified first-publication date; an Oiseau-Lyre discography (https://medieval.org/emfaq/cds/lol75.htm, after Davidson’s Lyrebird Rising) places the release in 1938 or 1939, and the label began issuing discs in December 1937. Either date is before 1963. The Gallica record marks its own digital copy as public domain; the Internet Archive item carries no licence. US first-publication evidence and US status are not established.

composer.epithet: Parisian harpsichordist and composer who played for Louis XIV as a child and published harpsichord suites, violin sonatas, cantatas and the opera Céphale et Procris.
facts: In Paris with her father, the organist Claude Jacquet; harpsichord and singing at court from the age of five
Played for Louis XIV as a child; three or four years at Madame de Montespan’s side; left the court on her marriage in 1684
Taught and gave concerts in her apartment on the Île Saint-Louis; married to the organist Marin de La Guerre
Harpsichord suites, trio and violin sonatas, cantatas, the opera Céphale et Procris and a lost Te Deum

quote.text: Finding in me at the age of five some disposition for the harpsichord, you ordered that care be taken to bring me up in it.
quote.source: Élisabeth Jacquet to Louis XIV, dedication of Les Pièces de clavessin, Paris, 1687; our translation

composer.background:
Élisabeth Jacquet was baptised in Paris on 17 March 1665. Her father, Claude Jacquet, was organist of Saint-Louis-en-l’Île, on the island in the Seine now called the Île Saint-Louis, and Catherine Cessac describes him as an excellent teacher. All four of his children became musicians: Pierre and Nicolas as organists, Anne as an instrumentalist in the household of Mademoiselle de Guise, and Élisabeth as a harpsichordist and singer. A great-uncle, Jehan Jacquet, and an uncle, also named Claude, were makers of musical instruments.

The dedication of her first printed book, in 1687, told Louis XIV how her training began. “Finding in me at the age of five some disposition for the harpsichord,” she wrote, “you ordered that care be taken to bring me up in it.” Cessac writes that she made her debut at court at that age, playing and singing before the king, and that he protected her and gave her the means to publish. Évrard Titon du Tillet, who gave her a long entry in his Parnasse françois of 1732, wrote that she was barely fifteen when she appeared at court, that the king took great pleasure in hearing her, and that Madame de Montespan kept her three or four years at her side to entertain herself and her visitors.
